The 3:14 AM express out of Blackwood Valley was less a train and more a long iron needle threading through the dark cloth of the mountain pass.

In Carriage Four, the overhead lights were dimmed to the color of weak tea, humming softly against the rhythmic *thump-thump, thump-thump* of the steel rails below. Julian sat with his knees pulled close, watching his own pale reflection overlaid against the dark, wet pine trees rushing past outside. He was thirty-two, but in the amber gloom of the compartment, he looked like a charcoal sketch of someone much older—sharp jawline, tired eyes, a faint crease between his brows that refused to smooth out even in sleep.

Across the narrow aisle sat an older woman who had not moved or spoken since they boarded at the terminal two hours ago. She wore a heavy coat of dark green wool, despite the dry warmth of the carriage, and her hands rested flat on top of a worn leather handbag in her lap. Her knuckles were swollen with the quiet geography of arthritis, yet her posture was remarkably upright, almost formal, as if she were waiting for an audience with someone important.

"It always rains on the ascent," she said suddenly. Her voice didn't startle him so much as it simply filled a space that had been waiting for sound. It was dry, clear, and carried the faint cadence of someone who grew up near the coast.

Julian pulled his gaze away from the glass. "Does it?"

"Every single time," she replied, her eyes fixed on the empty seat opposite her. "The clouds get caught in the upper gorge like wool caught on a rusty wire fence. If you're heading up to the crest, you either bring a good umbrella, or you accept the soak."

Julian adjusted the turned-up collar of his jacket. "I didn't bring an umbrella."

"Then you've chosen the soak," she said softly, a tiny flick of a smile gracing her thin, pale lips. "An honest choice, at least. Most people try to duck under the station overhangs that aren't there anymore."

They fell back into silence, but the air between them had irrevocably shifted. It was no longer the heavy, cautious silence of strangers stuck together on a late-night transport, but the lighter, speculative quiet of two people who had both left something heavy on the platform behind them.

"Are you going all the way to the coast?" Julian asked, needing the sound of a human voice to drown out the low rumble of the diesel engine beneath his feet.

"No," she said. "Just as far as the high bridge. My nephew has a house near the timber line. He burns birch wood in the stove. You can smell it three miles down the valley if the wind is coming from the west." She turned her head slightly toward him. Her eyes were a clear, startling hazel behind rimless spectacles. "And you? Where does your ticket say you're going?"

"I don't know yet," Julian admitted, rubbing his thumb against the fraying seam of his pocket. "I bought a ticket for the end of the line, but the conductor said the rails beyond the pass were undergoing night maintenance. He said we’d have to decide at the summit whether to transfer to the coastal bus or simply turn back."

"The conductor always says that," she murmured, a dry humor in her tone. "It keeps the passengers from falling entirely asleep before they reach the border."

Julian frowned slightly. "You've taken this route often?"

"Only when I need to leave a place that has finished with me."

The phrase hung in the narrow space of the carriage, heavy with a strange, undeniable weight. Julian looked down at his boots, muddy at the soles from his last aimless walk through the square of St. Jude-in-the-Fens. He thought of the town he had left that evening—the peeling yellow paint on the Victorian storefronts, the rusted iron gates of the public garden, the way the fog always smelled of damp coal ash and stagnant river water. It had felt like an open-air graveyard long before he walked into the station and bought his one-way pass.

"I left St. Jude’s tonight," Julian said, the confession slipping out before he could filter it. "It felt like it was dying. Like there was nothing left to breathe."

The woman tilted her head. "St. Jude’s? With the tall silver bell in the square's clocktower?"

"Yes. It hasn't rung in twenty years."

"Ah," she said, leaning back against the high headrest. "That's where you're mistaken. I was in St. Jude’s three days ago. The bell rang precisely at noon, six, and nine. The brass on the railings near the library was polished so bright you could see the gulls flying overhead reflected in the handrails. The baker on the corner of High Street was giving away hot currant buns because his eldest daughter had just given birth to healthy twins."

Julian stared at her, feeling a strange chill along his spine. "That’s impossible. High Street has been boarded up with plywood since the textile mill closed in ninety-eight. There hasn't been an open bakery there in my entire lifetime."

"It isn't a matter of *when*, young man," she said, her voice dropping into a tone of quiet instruction, the way a retired schoolteacher might explain an axiom of geometry to an unruly child. "It's a matter of what you were carrying when you walked down the street."

"I was carrying a leather satchel," he said defensively.

"You were carrying your grief," she corrected gently. "When you walk through a town with a heart full of soot, the windows look dirty. You see the rot in the window sill, not the bright red geranium resting on it. St. Jude’s isn't dead. It’s just waiting for someone who remembers how to look at it without mourning what isn't there anymore."

The train lurched violently as it hit a steep, sweeping curve, the iron wheels screaming in high-pitched protest against the bend. Outside, the dark, tangled pines gave way to sheer granite faces slick with black water. The rain lashed against the double pane in sudden, rhythmic gusts, like handfuls of fine sand thrown against the glass.

Julian felt a sharp, hollow ache in his chest—the familiar pang he’d been fleeing since Tuesday, when the lawyer's letter had arrived, sealed in heavy cream paper, confirming what he’d known for months. He had spent three agonizing years trying to preserve a house that didn't want to stand, a family legacy that had turned to grey dust between his fingers.

"How do you drop it?" he asked, his voice barely louder than the hum of the electric heater beneath his seat. "The soot."

The woman reached down and unlatched her handbag with a soft *clack*. She reached inside and pulled out a small, smooth river stone, no larger than a plum, worn flat and soft by centuries of running water. She held it out on the open palm of her hand.

"You don't drop it," she said. "You just stop pretending it's gold. You put it in your pocket, or you leave it on a windowsill for the next traveler to find, and you step onto the train."

Julian looked at the stone. In the amber glow of Carriage Four, it looked utterly ordinary, entirely heavy, and entirely real.

"What's your name?" he asked softly.

"Evelyn," she said, pulling her hand back. "And yours?"

"Julian."

"Well, Julian," Evelyn said, placing the stone carefully in the middle of the small wooden table between their seats. "The high bridge is thirty seconds away. The fog always clears right at the peak. Look out the window when we cross. Don't look down at the river in the dark. Look out at the horizon."

The train began to decelerate, the heavy diesel engine exhaling a long, shuddering sigh of air brakes that rattled the floorboards under their feet. Outside, the black wall of granite suddenly gave way to vast, empty space. The rain stopped instantly, as if cut by a knife. Through the double glass, far out in the immense, moonlit expanse beyond the gorge, the dark clouds parted, revealing a cold, silver coastline stretching toward a sky full of impossibly bright, silent stars.

Julian looked out into the vast open night. He didn't turn back.
